newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Refugee voting deal highlights Bosnia's divisions.
newsitem.headline: Refugee voting deal highlights Bosnia's divisions.

text.p: A deal enabling tens of thousands of victims of Bosnia's ethnic cleansing to return to their home districts to vote in countrywide elections has highlighted the country's deep divisions.
Bosnia's Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders announced the plan on Monday at a rare joint press conference intended to show reconciliation was slowly, but surely underway.

In a joint statement, interior ministers of the Bosnian Serb Republic and Moslem-Croat Federation said they had agreed 19 "voters' routes" crossing ethnic boundary lines on which full security would be ensured.
"Demonstrations and gatherings along these routes will be prohibited on election day...We will encourage all our citizens to use these routes on election day September 14," the statement said.

But in true Balkan fashion the event backfired after Bosnian Serb Interior Minister Dragan Kijac said only people using these routes would be allowed to vote -- a breach of the Dayton accords which foresee complete freedom of movement.

"Any operation does require certain prohibitions from a football match to Olympic games, citizens cannot do what they want, their rights are being limited," Kijac said, adding: "This is not a restriction of freedom of movement, this is just a security measure."

Critics say freedom of movement does not exist in any meaningful way in Bosnia and the upcoming elections are simply going to consolidate the country's ethnic divide, making it more likely to become permanent.

Immediately after the press conference Alex Ivanko, spokesman for the International Police Task Force, said Kijac had clarified his position, saying he simply could not guarantee the security of people using other routes.
At least 65,000 people are expected to cross from federation territory and perhaps 100,000 from Serb-held Bosnia and Serbia.

Officials say it could be many more -- hundreds of thousands were driven out of their homes in ethnic cleansing during Bosnia's 1992-95 war and they fear an unsupervised return to vote could spark widespread unrest and wreck the polls.
Kijac said the refugees were going only to vote and would have to return afterwards to allow others to use the same buses.
One international official monitoring the poll said he was very concerned by the deal.

"It does not guarantee the freedom of movement, and is by and large restricting the freedom of movement on election day...People will be forced to use buses only and who will provide those buses?" he said.

The official said if the buses, as is widely expected to be the case, are provided by political parties, then it raised the question of neutrality and disenfranchising of many voters who are not willing to accept such transport.

Monitors from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) which is organising the poll welcomed the deal, but stressed it did not mean other crossings would be closed to people who decided to set out for their old homes independently.
Colum Murphy, spokesman for international peace coordinator Carl Bildt, praised the deal, saying it in no way conflicted with the Dayton peace accords.
